## What social science is for {#what-are-we-doing-when-we-do-social-science}

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment}
Making **claims about the world** that could turn out to be wrong – and saying how we would know.
:::

::: {.fragment}
A claim is offered to others so that they can **check it, use it, argue with it, build on it**.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Science depends on that handover, and everything that follows is about whether it works.
:::
::::

::: notes
I want to start with a question that is seldom asked out loud, namely what we are doing when we do social science. We make claims about the world that could turn out to be wrong, together with some statement of how we would find out. And we publish a claim so that other people can check it, use it, argue with it and build on it. Science depends on that handover, since a finding that nobody else can examine remains an assertion. When we ask whether social science is in trouble, then, the question is quite specific: whether the handover works, and whether someone else can pick a finding up and do something with it.
:::

## False positives and forking paths {#three-arguments-that-made-people-nervous .smaller}

::: {.small}
- **The theory, 2005.** With small studies, small true effects, flexible designs and many teams chasing the same question, most published findings in a field can be false with nobody breaking any rules [@Ioannidis2005WhyMostPublished]
- **The demonstration, 2011.** Give researchers only the flexibility they legitimately have – which cases to drop, which covariates to keep, when to stop collecting – and a **false-positive rate of 5% becomes over 60%** [@SimmonsEtAl2011FalsePositivePsychology]
- **The subtlety, 2014.** You do not need many tests. In a **garden of forking paths**, a single test *chosen after looking at the data* already has the wrong p-value [@GelmanLoken2014StatisticalCrisisScience]
:::

::: notes
Three arguments made people nervous, and I take them in the order of how uncomfortable they are. Ioannidis in 2005 made the theoretical case: with small studies, small true effects, flexible designs and many teams chasing the same question, most published findings in a field can be false without anybody breaking a rule. Simmons, Nelson and Simonsohn then demonstrated it in 2011, showing that the flexibility that researchers legitimately have can push a false-positive rate of five per cent above sixty. They made the point by 'showing', with real participants and real statistics, that listening to a Beatles song makes people younger. Gelman and Loken added the subtlety that I find hardest to shake off, which is that you do not need to run many tests for this to happen, because a single test chosen after looking at the data already has the wrong p-value.
:::

## Evidence from replications and many-analysts studies {#and-then-people-counted .smaller}

::: {.small}
- **100 psychology studies**, replicated with high power and the original materials: **97%** of the originals were significant, **36%** of the replications were, and effect sizes roughly **halved** [@OpenScienceCollaboration2015EstimatingReproducibilityPsychological]
- **161 researchers, 73 teams, one hypothesis** on immigration and support for social policy: **1,253** models, and no convergence on either sign or significance [@BreznauEtAl2022ObservingManyResearchers]
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Different fields and different designs. In the first, **most findings were not significant again in new samples**; in the second, **the result depended on who ran the analysis.**
:::

::: notes
Then people stopped arguing and counted. The Open Science Collaboration replicated a hundred psychology studies with high power and the original materials. Ninety-seven per cent of the original studies had reported a significant result, against thirty-six per cent of the replications, and the effect sizes came back at about half their original size; this is the study that took the phrase 'replication crisis' out of methodology seminars. The second study is closer to our own field: seventy-three teams, a hundred and sixty-one researchers, one hypothesis about immigration and support for social policy, more than twelve hundred models between them, and no agreement on the sign of the effect, let alone on its significance. [advance] The fields and the designs differ. In the first study most findings were not significant again in new samples, while in the second the result depended on who ran the analysis.
:::

## Incentives and questionable research practices {#it-is-not-mostly-fraud .smaller}

::: {.small}
Fraud exists, but it is rare. The mechanism behind these results is **ordinary and structural**:

- Journals reward novel, clean, significant results – so that is what gets written up
- Every analysis contains dozens of small defensible choices, and the analyst makes them while looking at the data
- Nobody publishes the twelve specifications that did not work; the reader sees one
- Data and code are usually not available, so nobody can check any of it
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Ask researchers anonymously, with an incentive to answer truthfully, and a **majority admit** to at least one of these ordinary practices [@JohnEtAl2012MeasuringPrevalenceQuestionable]
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
None of these steps requires a dishonest person, so the problem cannot be fixed by hiring better people.
:::

::: notes
This is not mostly a story about fraud, which exists but is rare and is not what these numbers measure. The mechanism is ordinary and structural. Journals want novel, clean and significant results, so that is what gets written up. Every analysis involves dozens of small choices, each defensible on its own, which the analyst makes while looking at the data, nobody publishes the twelve specifications that did not work, and in most cases neither the data nor the code are available for anyone to check. [advance] John, Loewenstein and Prelec asked researchers anonymously, with a scoring scheme that rewarded truthful answers, and a majority admitted to at least one of these practices. [advance] None of these steps requires a dishonest person, which is why hiring better people cannot fix the problem. [pause] Suppose, then, that you hired the best people that you could find and gave them all the same data and the same question.
:::

## The red-card study {#twenty-nine-teams-one-question .smaller}

::: {.small}
**The question.** Are football referees more likely to give red cards to dark-skinned players than to light-skinned ones?

**The data.** One dataset, sent to everyone: 2,053 players in the top divisions of England, Germany, France and Spain, the 3,147 referees they played under, and **146,028 player–referee pairs**. Skin tone rated from profile photographs by two coders who did not know the research question.

**The design.** Twenty-nine teams analysed it independently. They reviewed each other's approaches *before* anyone had seen a result, revised, and only then compared answers.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The SCORE robustness study [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness], from which this workshop's case studies come, applied the same approach to a hundred published studies.
:::

::: {.src}
@SilberzahnEtAl2018ManyAnalystsOne
:::

::: notes
Silberzahn and colleagues ran something very close to that experiment, in a study published in twenty eighteen. The question was whether football referees are more likely to give red cards to dark-skinned players than to light-skinned ones. Every team received the same data: two thousand and fifty-three players in the top divisions of England, Germany, France and Spain, the three thousand one hundred and forty-seven referees under whom the players had played, and a hundred and forty-six thousand player–referee pairs, with skin tone rated from photographs by two coders who did not know the research question. Twenty-nine teams analysed the data independently, reviewed one another's approaches before anyone had seen a result, revised, and only then compared answers, so that no team could tune its method towards a number that it liked. [advance] The SCORE robustness study, in which I was one of the analysts, applied the same approach to a hundred published studies.
:::

## The twenty-nine estimates {#all-twenty-nine-side-by-side}

```{r}
#| label: silberzahn-forest
#| fig-width: 9.6
#| fig-height: 5.0
# Figure 3 of the paper, rebuilt from the authors' published values rather than
# reproduced as an image: every team, every interval, grouped by the response
# distribution it assumed. Colour is ours – the original is monochrome – and
# marks whether the interval excludes 1. Teams 21 and 27 have intervals running
# to 11.5 and 78.7; the published figure truncates both and asterisks them, and
# so does this.
CLIP <- 3.2
szf <- silberzahn29 |>
  datawizard::data_modify(hi_draw = pmin(or_hi, CLIP),
         lab = paste0(team, ". ", tidy_approach(approach))) |>
  datawizard::data_arrange(c("distribution", "or")) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(lab = factor(lab, levels = rev(lab)))

ggplot2::ggplot(szf, ggplot2::aes(or, lab, colour = significant)) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "longdash", colour = grey_mid) +
  ggplot2::geom_errorbarh(ggplot2::aes(xmin = or_lo, xmax = hi_draw), height = 0, linewidth = 0.55) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 2.4) +
  ggplot2::geom_text(data = datawizard::data_filter(szf, or_hi > CLIP), ggplot2::aes(x = CLIP + 0.04, label = "*"),
            size = 5, vjust = 0.75, show.legend = FALSE) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = ncl_blue, `FALSE` = d_red),
                      breaks = c("TRUE", "FALSE"), name = NULL,
                      labels = c("interval excludes 1", "interval includes 1")) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3),
                     expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = c(0.01, 0.03))) +
  ggplot2::coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.42, CLIP + 0.1)) +
  ggplot2::facet_grid(distribution ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y", switch = "y") +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "odds ratio", y = NULL,
       caption = paste("Above 1: dark-skinned players red-carded more often.",
                       "* interval runs past the edge (teams 21 and 27).")) +
  theme_slide(11) +
  ggplot2::theme(plot.caption = ggplot2::element_text(hjust = 1, colour = "grey45", size = 9,
                                    margin = ggplot2::margin(t = 4)),
        legend.position = "top", legend.justification = "right",
        legend.margin = ggplot2::margin(0, 0, -6, 0),
        legend.text = ggplot2::element_text(size = 10, colour = "grey25"),
        panel.grid.major.y = ggplot2::element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.x = ggplot2::element_line(colour = "grey92"),
        strip.placement = "outside",
        strip.text.y.left = ggplot2::element_text(angle = 0, face = "bold",
                                         colour = ncl_blue, hjust = 1),
        axis.text.y = ggplot2::element_text(colour = "grey25", hjust = 0, size = 8.5),
        panel.spacing.y = ggplot2::unit(0.45, "lines"))
```

::: {.src}
@SilberzahnEtAl2018ManyAnalystsOne, Figure 3, rebuilt from the published values at osf.io/gvm2z.
:::

::: notes
These are the twenty-nine analyses of one dataset. The odds ratios run from nought point eight nine, which would mean that dark-skinned players were red-carded slightly less often, to two point nine three, with a median of one point three one. Twenty of the twenty-nine intervals exclude one and nine do not, so about two thirds of the teams found an effect and a third did not, on identical data. [pause] The left column groups the teams by the distribution that they assumed for the outcome: linear, logistic, Poisson, and two that fit none of the three. Each team made that decision for itself, and each choice was defensible. On the second day you make the same kind of decision yourselves, on the specification menu of your case study, where the model is one of the groups of decisions.
:::
